rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause that their hands are tied and they are cursed may be a report or a curse; “for what they said” may mean this utterance or all their impermissible claims about God, including this one.
rows.anchor: غلت أيديهم ولعنوا بما قالوا يحتمل أن يكون خبرا وأن يكون دعاء

rows.speaker: أبو السمال
rows.claim: Abū al-Sammāl reads the ʿayn with sukūn; the cited verse of poetry supports easing the vowel between two ḍammas.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو السمال: بسكون العين كما قالوا: في عصر عصرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Orthodox theologians hold that God is neither body nor limb, unlike creation, without modality or spatial location, and untouched by created events.
rows.anchor: معتقد أهل الحق أن الله تعالى ليس بجسم ولا جارحة له، ولا يشبه بشيء من خلقه

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most interpreters take God’s two outstretched hands as a metaphor for abundant generosity; the spending context confirms that reading, as do Arabic idioms for openhandedness and miserliness.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على أن هذا استعارة عن جوده وإنعامه السابغ، وأضاف ذلك إلى اليدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic usage freely assigns a hand to an abstraction, so a hand image can mean generosity even where no physical hand exists; Labīd’s line supplies a poetic example.
rows.anchor:
وقد استعملت العرب ذلك حيث لا يكون قال الشاعر:
جاد الحمى بسط اليدين بوابل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the dual intensifies the rebuttal and denotes maximal generosity: a generous person gives with both hands; Abū Ḥayyān calls this explanation excellent.
rows.anchor: ليكون رد قولهم وإنكاره أبلغ وأدل على إثبات غاية السخاء له ونفي البخل عنه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the two hands as two blessings; other proposed pairs are religion and worldly life, sound faculties and provision, outward and inward blessings, or rain and vegetation.
rows.anchor: وقيل عن ابن عباس: يداه نعمتاه، فقيل: هما مجازان عن نعمة الدين ونعمة الدنيا

rows.speaker: جمهور الأمة
rows.claim: The majority interpret other expressions that might imply embodiment, such as God’s hands, eyes, or face, according to Arabic usage and figurative rhetoric.
rows.anchor: فجمهور الأمة أنها تفسر على قوانين اللغة ومجاز الاستعارة وغير ذلك من أفانين الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The increase in many of them is tied to revelation about stoning and blood money concerning Banū al-Naḍīr.
rows.anchor: وليزيدن بني النضير ما أنزل إليك من ربك من أمر الرجم والدماء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: “Many” is interpreted as the Jewish scholars.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد بالكثير علماء اليهود

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Their persistence in disbelief is itself described as an increase in disbelief.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إقامتهم على الكفر زيادة منهم في الكفر

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid take “between them” to mean Jews and Christians, since both groups were just named and both are addressed as People of Scripture.
rows.anchor:
عائد على
اليهود والنصارى، لأنه جرى ذكرهم في قوله: لا تتخذوا اليهود والنصارى أولياء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view confines the pronoun to Jews, whose sects include Jabrites, Qadarites, monotheists, and anthropomorphists, alongside several Christian sects.
rows.anchor: هو عائد على اليهود، إذ هم جبرية وقدرية وموحدة ومشبهة، وكذلك فرق النصارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān reads the clause as lasting mutual hostility that prevents Jews and Christians from uniting to fight or harm the Prophet and his followers; he treats this as a prediction borne out in Islamic history.
rows.anchor: متباغضين متعادين، فلا يمكن اجتماع كلمتهم على قتالك، ولا يقدرون على ضررك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī similarly says they remain divided, with scattered hearts and no agreement or mutual support.
rows.anchor: فكلهم أبدا مختلف وقلوبهم شتى، لا يقع اتفاق بينهم، ولا تعاضد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Enmity is narrower than hatred: every enemy hates, but one may hate someone without being that person’s enemy.
rows.anchor: والعداوة أخص من البغضاء، لأن كل عدو مبغض، وقد يبغض من ليس بعدو

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes active enmity, which produces action and war, from hatred that stays within the heart.
rows.anchor: وكأن العداوة شيء يشهد يكون عنه عمل وحرب، والبغضاء لا تتجاوز النفوس

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some take the war-fire literally as a beacon system: Arabs lit fires on heights to summon armies, and in al-Andalus Muslims used a chain of watchers to warn of Roman attacks.
rows.anchor: كانت تتواعد للقتال، وعلامتهم إيقاد نار على جبل أو ربوة، فيتبادرون

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another literal explanation says armies lit fires at night when they faced one another, to guard against a surprise attack.
rows.anchor: إذا تراءى الجمعان وتنازل العسكران أوقدوا بالليل نارا مخافة البيات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further explanation says they lit a fire when pledging themselves to pursue war earnestly.
rows.anchor: كانوا إذا تحالفوا على الجد في حربهم أوقدوا نارا وتحالفوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the literal reading, God extinguishes their fire by casting terror into them; they fear an attack on their homes and withdraw, with the extinguishing attributed to God as the primary cause.
rows.anchor: يكون معنى إطفائها أنه ألقى الله الرعب في قلوبهم فخافوا أن يغشوا في منازلهم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most interpreters read the fire figuratively: kindling means displaying hatred, plots, schemes, treachery, and fighting against believers; extinguishing means God frustrates these plans through fear, division, and loss of resolve.
rows.anchor: إيقاد النار عبارة عن إظهار الحقد والكيد والمكر بالمؤمنين والاغتيال والقتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the figurative reading, whenever they seek war they are defeated and receive no divine victory; Islam arrived while they were under Persian rule.
rows.anchor:
فهم لا يريدون محاربة أحد إلا غلبوا
وقهروا، ولم يقم لهم نصر من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One historical account says that after opposing the Jews, God sent Nebuchadnezzar against them, then a Byzantine ruler, then the Magians, and finally the Muslims as they continued to corrupt themselves.
rows.anchor: خالفوا اليهود فبعث الله عليهم بختنصر، ثم أفسدوا فسلط الله عليهم بطريق الرومي

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some call the fire a simile for their fierce exertion in war and burning hearts; extinguishing represents their humiliation and defeat in every theater.
rows.anchor: هذا مثل ضرب لاجتهادهم في المحاربة، والتهاب شواظ قلوبهم، وغليان صدورهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the verse reassures the Messenger that whenever they fight him he will prevail, and refers to the Jews present in the Prophet’s time.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: هي تبشير للرسول بأنهم كلما حاربوه نصر عليهم، وإشارة إلى حاضريه من اليهود

rows.speaker: السدي والربيع وغيرهما
rows.claim: Al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ, and others apply it to the ancestors: their rule has fallen, no banner will rise for them, and they will fight only from fortified towns.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي والربيع وغيرهما: هي إخبار عن أسلافهم منذ عصور هد الله ملكهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says Jews are found to be among the most humiliated people wherever they are encountered.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: لا تلقى اليهود ببلدة إلا وجدتهم من أذل الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Striving” may literally mean going from place to place to manifest corruption, though the apparent meaning is working and exerting themselves to plot against Islam and erase the Messenger’s mention from their books.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه يراد به العمل. والفعل أي: يجتهدون، في كيد أهل الإسلام ومحو ذكر الرسول من كتبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The earth” can mean the earth generally or the land of the Ḥijāz, with the latter taking the definite article as a reference to a known land.
rows.anchor: والأرض يجوز أن يراد بها الجنس، أو أرض الحجاز، فتكون أل فيه للعهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil explain their corruption as sins.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس ومقاتل: فسادهم بالمعاصي

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says their corruption is resisting Islam and removing mention of the Messenger from their books.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: بدفع الإسلام ومحو ذكر الرسول من كتبهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other explanations identify their corruption as bloodshed and violating inviolable matters, disbelief, or injustice; Abū Ḥayyān says these views are close in meaning.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بسفك الدماء واستحلال المحارم. وقيل: بالكفر. وقيل: بالظلم، وكل هذه الأقوال متقاربة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The corrupters” can be generic or refer specifically to this group; saying God does not love them euphemistically means He withholds favor, so they are punished, since there is no middle state between reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: وانتفاء المحبة كناية عن كونه لا يعود عليهم بفضله وإحسانه، فهؤلاء يثيبهم. وإذا لم يثبهم فهو معاقبهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some take the People of Scripture addressed as their forebears, with contemporaries included by implication; Abū Ḥayyān’s apparent view is that the contemporaries of the Messenger are addressed to encourage conversion.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أنهم معاصر والرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم، وفي ذلك ترغيب لهم في الدخول في الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two conditions lead to two rewards: faith expiates prior sins because Islam erases what came before, while fearing God through obedience and avoiding prohibitions leads to Paradise.
rows.anchor: قابل الإيمان بتكفير السيئات إذ الإسلام يجب ما قبله، وترتب على التقوى وهي امتثال الأوامر واجتناب المناهي دخول جنة النعيم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: “They feared God” is variously glossed as not rejecting Muhammad and Jesus, avoiding the sins behind their curse, or avoiding idolatry.
rows.anchor:
وقيل: واتقوا أي: الكفر بمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم،
وبعيسى عليه السلام. وقيل: المعاصي التي لعنوا بسببها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says belief in Muhammad and his revelation must be joined to piety; then sins are forgiven and they enter Paradise with Muslims, showing both the severity of their sins and God’s broad mercy and open repentance.
rows.anchor: لكفرنا عنهم تلك السيئات، فلم نؤاخذهم بها، ولأدخلناهم مع المسلمين الجنة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī adds that faith does not save or bring felicity unless accompanied by piety; Abū Ḥayyān marks this condition of faith’s success as Muʿtazilite doctrine.
rows.anchor: وأن الإيمان لا ينجي ولا يسعد إلا مشفوعا بالتقوى كما قال الحسن: هذا العمود فأين الأطناب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise for upholding the Torah and Gospel urges the People of Scripture to believe and follow their books, offering worldly provision in addition to the afterlife reward promised just before; the lasting afterlife is given priority.
rows.anchor: هذا استدعاء لإيمانهم، وتنبيه لهم على اتباع ما في كتبهم، وترغيب لهم في عاجل الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Upholding the Torah and Gospel means displaying their rulings, their prophecy of the Messenger, and the command to follow him, as one “opens” or activates a market.
rows.anchor: ومعنى إقامة التوراة والإنجيل: هو إظهار ما انطوت عليه من الأحكام والتبشير بالرسول والأمر باتباعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mention of the Gospel shows that Christians are included among the People of Scripture.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: والإنجيل دليل على دخول النصارى في لفظ أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: “What was sent down to them from their Lord” may mean the full range of divine books, including Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, said to be full of prophecies of the Messenger, or it may mean the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله: وما أنزل إليهم من ربهم، العموم في الكتب الإلهية مثل: كتاب أشعياء، وكتاب حزقيل

rows.speaker: الطبري والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zajjāj take provision from above and below as a metaphor for abundant, all-encompassing sustenance.
rows.anchor: أنه استعارة عن سبوغ النعم عليهم، وتوسعة الرزق عليهم، كما يقال: قد عمه الرزق من فرقه إلى قدمه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, and al-Suddī say heaven would give rain and blessing and earth its vegetation, as promised elsewhere.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وقتادة، والسدي: لأعطتهم السماء مطرها وبركتها، والأرض نباتها

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqāsh interprets provision from above as provision of Paradise and provision below as worldly provision from the earth’s plants.
rows.anchor: وذكر النقاش من فوقهم من

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other glosses make the upper provision abundant fruit trees and the lower provision productive crops, or ripe orchard fruit to pick from branches and the ground.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من فوقهم كثرة الأشجار المثمرة، ومن تحت أرجلهم الزرع المغلة

rows.speaker: تاج القراء
rows.claim: Tāj al-Qurrāʾ says the upper provision comes from leaders and kings, the lower from common people; “eating” stands for taking because it is life’s most important need.
rows.anchor: من فوقهم ما يأتيهم من كبرائهم وملوكهم، ومن تحت أرجلهم ما يأتيهم من سفلتهم وعوامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “among them” refers to the People of Scripture; “a community” means a small group contrasted with the many, and moderation derives from qasd, balance, with a form suggesting exertion or acquisition.
rows.anchor: الضمير في منهم يعود على أهل الكتاب. والأمة هنا يراد بها الجماعة القليلة للمقابلة لها بقوله: وكثير منهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation identifies the moderate group as believers from both communities, including ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions and forty-eight Christians; their moderation is belief in God.
rows.anchor: قيل: هم مؤمنو الفريقين عبد الله بن سلام وأصحابه، وثمانية وأربعون من النصارى

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the moderate group consists of Muslim People of Scripture, both ancient and contemporary.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: المقتصدة مسلمة أهل الكتاب قديما وحديثا

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies them as the obedient People of Scripture.
rows.anchor:
ونحوه قول ابن زيد:
هم أهل طاعة الله من أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: الزجاج وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj and others say these are groups who did not oppose the prophets as obstinately as their militant opponents.
rows.anchor: وذكر الزجاج وغيره: أنها الطوائف التي لم تناصب الأنبياء مناصبة المتمردين المجاهدين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī understands the group’s moderation as a lesser degree of hostility to the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: مقتصدة حالها أمم في عداوة الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says some Israelites were moderate about Jesus, affirming him as God’s servant, messenger, and spirit from Him; others exaggerated by calling him divine, while most Israelites said he was an ordinary person of illegitimate birth.
rows.anchor: من بني إسرائيل من يقتصد في عيسى فيقول: هو عبد الله ورسوله وروح منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān leaves open whether moderation concerns their view of Jesus, their opposition to prophets, or their faith; if opposition, it may be to the Messenger alone or to all prophets, and if faith, to converts from both eras or only one.
rows.anchor: فتخلص في الاقتصاد أهو في حق عيسى؟ أو في المناصبة؟ أو في الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax marks moderation as a lasting attribute while the first group remains scripturally affiliated by origin; the second group’s condemnation is the predicate because some may later convert and cease to fit it.
rows.anchor: فأخبر عنهم بأنهم من أهل الكتاب في الأصل، ثم قد تزول هذه النسبة بالإسلام

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats “ساء” as an uninflected verb of blame, yielding an exclamation like “How evil their deeds are!”
rows.anchor:
واختار الزمخشري في ساء أن تكون التي لا تنصرف، فإن فيه التعجب كأنه قيل:
ما أسوأ عملهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers inflected “ساء يسوء” but also allows it as an uninflected verb like niʿma and biʾsa; the inflected reading needs an implied object, the frozen reading a specification.
rows.anchor: واختار ابن عطية أن تكون المتصرفة تقول: ساء الأمر يسوء، وأجاز أن تكون غير المتصرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noble address commands delivery of what was revealed; because the Messenger had already delivered it, Abū Ḥayyān reads the command as requiring him to continue doing so.
rows.anchor: هذا نداء بالصفة الشريفة التي هي أشرف أوصاف الجنس الإنساني، وأمر بتبليغ ما أنزل إليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says he must convey all revelation without watching anyone or fearing harm.
rows.anchor: جميع ما أنزل إليك، وأي شيء أنزل غير مراقب في تبليغه أحدا ولا خائف

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the command requires complete delivery without hesitation or fear; the message criticized unbelievers and their conditions, so they caused hardship and could be feared before this verse.
rows.anchor: أمر من الله لرسوله بالتبليغ على الاستيفاء والكمال، لأنه قد قال: بلغ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās transmits the Prophet’s account that, when commissioned, he felt burdened and expected some people to reject him, so this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: لما بعثني الله برسالته ضقت بها ذرعا وعرفت أن من الناس من يكذبني

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say this specifically commanded conveying the stoning and blood-money rulings that Jews altered in the Torah and Christians in the Gospel.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو أمر بتبليغ خاص أي: ما أنزل إليك من الرجم والقصاص الذي غيره اليهود

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another specific-revelation view links the verse to the command about Zaynab bint Jaḥsh and the Prophet’s marriage to her.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أمر بتبليغ أمر زينب بنت جحش ونكاحها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says it commanded communicating the call to jihād and not abandoning it for anyone’s sake.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بتبليغ الجهاد والحث عليه، وأن لا يتركه لأجل أحد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view ties it to criticizing idols, which the Prophet had refrained from doing after the warning not to insult those invoked besides God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أمر بتبليغ معائب آلهتهم، إذ كان قد سكت عند نزول قوله: ولا تسبوا الذين يدعون من دون الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān’s apparent reading is a general command to convey all revelation, especially about Jews and Christians, with God securing the Messenger from their schemes; the surrounding passage makes a disconnected special occasion unlikely.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أنه تعالى أمنه من مكر اليهود والنصارى، وأمره بتبليغ ما أنزل إليه في أمرهم وغيره

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī offers two readings of “if you do not, you have not delivered”: withholding the whole message makes it as though no messenger was sent, or withholding even one word is treated like concealing all of it, by analogy with the gravity of killing one person.
rows.anchor: أنه إذا لم يمتثل أمر الله في تبليغ الرسالة وكتمها كلها كأنه لم يبعث رسولا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī’s second explanation is that the threat of punishment resulting from concealment is stated by naming its cause; he cites a divine warning to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: أن يراد فإن لم تفعل ذلك ما يوجبه كتمان الوحي كله من العقاب، فوضع السبب موضع المسبب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says leaving anything is like leaving the whole message, so what was delivered would count for nothing; “if you do not” means if you fail to complete delivery.
rows.anchor: أي إن تركت شيئا فكأنك قد تركت الكل، وصار ما بلغت غير معتد به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poetic line illustrates that failing to give what counts as a real gift leaves neither blame nor praise; the comparison concerns failure to deliver a sufficient amount.
rows.anchor: سئلت فلم تبخل ولم تعط نائلا ... فسيان لا ذم عليك ولا حمد

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reports the majority’s view that failure to deliver any one part counts as failure to deliver the whole, but objects that partial omission and total omission are unequal.
rows.anchor: أجاب الجمهور بإن لم تبلغ واحدا منها كنت كمن لم يبلغ شيئا. وهذا ضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Rāzī’s criticism: the majority mean the parts depend on one another as a single message, so incomplete delivery does not count as delivery of that whole.
rows.anchor: إن بعضها ليس أولى بالأداء من بعض، فإذا لم تؤد بعضها فكأنك أغفلت أداها جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no impossibility in God assigning a great punishment to a small sin or forgiving a great one; He is not questioned about what He does, unlike those questioned.
rows.anchor: ولله تعالى أن يرتب على الذنب اليسير العذاب العظيم، وله تعالى أن يعفو عن الذنب العظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Different legal penalties show that God may assign different consequences: concealed theft incurs amputation and restitution, whereas taking by force requires restitution alone.
rows.anchor: رتب على من أخذ شيئا بالاختفاء والتستر، قطع اليد مع رد ما أخذه أو قيمته

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī prefers reading the wording as an emphatic rhetorical formula like “I am Abū al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry”: saying the Messenger failed to deliver is the strongest possible threat and warning.
rows.anchor: والأصح عندي أن يقال: إن هذا خرج على قانون قوله: أنا أبو النجم وشعري شعري

rows.speaker: نافع وابن عامر وأبو بكر
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū Bakr read “His messages” in the plural.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن عامر وأبو بكر: رسالاته على الجمع

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة
rows.claim: The other seven canonical readers use the singular “His message.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة: على التوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s protection means the Prophet need not fear in delivery: people cannot kill him through conspiracy or assassination, nor capture or overpower him.
rows.anchor: أي لا تبال في التبليغ، فإن الله يعصمك فليس لهم تسليط على قتلك لا بمؤامرة

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb says the verse was revealed after a Bedouin drew the Prophet’s sword to kill him; the man was Ghawrath ibn al-Ḥārith during the expedition of Dhāt al-Riqāʿ.
rows.anchor:
نزلت بسبب الأعرابي الذي اخترط سيف النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ليقتله
انتهى، وهو غورث بن الحرث

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes report that Abū Ṭālib had men of Banū Hāshim guard the Prophet until the verse came, after which the Prophet said God had protected him from jinn and humans and no guard was needed.
rows.anchor: أن أبا طالب كان يرسل رجالا من بني هاشم يحرسونه حتى نزل قوله: والله يعصمك من الناس

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the Prophet feared Quraysh; after revelation he reclined and repeated that whoever wished could try to overcome him.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: كان يهاب قريشا فلما نزلت استلقى وقال: «من شاء فليخذلني مرتين أو ثلاثا

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة
rows.claim: Abū Umāma reports the Rukāna story: the pagan wrestler lost three bouts to the Prophet, asked for a sign, saw a split tree return together, and later the Prophet recited this verse after Abū Bakr and ʿUmar said they feared Rukāna might attack him.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو أمامة حديث ركانة من: ولد هاشم مشركا أفتك الناس وأشدهم، تصارع هو والرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited poetic line illustrates the complete use of “to be” in the sense of existing or occurring, which Abū Ḥayyān takes as the grammar here.
rows.anchor:
حسبت التقى والجود خير تجارة ... رباحا إذا ما المرء أصبح ثاقلا
وتكون هنا تامة

rows.speaker: جماعة
rows.claim: Some say Israel’s repentance was their return to Jerusalem after the first expulsion, while blindness and deafness describe their condition; others say they were veiled by desire and failed to see truth or hear God’s call.
rows.anchor: قالت جماعة: توبتهم هذه ردهم إلى بيت المقدس بعد الإخراج الأول وعماهم وصممهم

rows.speaker: جماعة
rows.claim: Other groups identify their repentance with the missions of Jesus or Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وقالت جماعة: توبتهم ببعث عيسى عليه السلام. وقالت جماعة: بعث محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another chronology places the first episode in the times of Zechariah, John, and Jesus, when many were guided, and the second in Muhammad’s time, when some believed but many remained unbelievers.
rows.anchor: الأول: في زمان زكريا ويحيى وعيسى عليهم الصلاة والسلام، ولتوفيق كثير منهم للإيمان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī identifies the first episode as calf worship and repentance, and the second as demanding to see God, which he calls impossible in God’s attributes; Abū Ḥayyān notes his Muʿtazilite rejection of the vision of God.
rows.anchor: الأول عبادة العجل ثم التوبة عنه، ثم الثاني بطلب الرؤية وهي محال غير معقول في صفات الله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view says the first episode followed Moses and was repented through Jesus’s mission, while the second was disbelief in the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الأول بعد موسى ثم تاب عليهم ببعث عيسى. والثاني بالكفر بالرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān’s apparent reading is that Israel assumed descent from prophets exempted them from testing, but their disobedience brought blindness and deafness; after affliction led them back to obedience, God accepted their repentance.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن المعنى حسب بنو إسرائيل حيث هم أبناء الرسل والأنبياء أن لا يبتلوا إذا عصوا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blindness comes first because turning from revealed law first prevents seeing its bearer; if they did see him, they then refused to hear his words.
rows.anchor: وبدئ بالعمى لأنه أول ما يعرض للمعرض عن الشرائع أن لا يبصر من أتاه بها من عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because they had guidance before straying, the acts of blindness and deafness are attributed to them; for those never guided, God is said to make them deaf and blind, as in another verse.
rows.anchor: ولما كانوا قبل ذلك على طريق الهداية، ثم عرض لهم الضلال، نسب الفعل إليهم وأسند لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “then God turned to them” rather than “then they repented” emphasizes God’s care and gentleness toward them.
rows.anchor: وأسند الفعل الشريف إلى الله تعالى في قوله: ثم تاب الله عليهم لم يأت، ثم تابوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunction fa indicates that disobedience and straying followed their presumption, while thumma indicates that they persisted in error for a time before God accepted repentance.
rows.anchor: وفي العطف بالفاء دليل على أنهم يعقب الحسبان عصيانهم وضلالهم، وفي العطف بثم دليل على أنهم تمادوا

rows.speaker: النخعي وابن وثاب
rows.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī and Ibn Waththāb read the verbs with ḍamma on ʿayn and ṣād and a light mīm; Abū Ḥayyān treats this as a rare verb pattern, comparable to forms like “zukkima” and “ḥumma.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ النخعي وابن وثاب بضم العين والصاد وتخفيف الميم من عموا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the rounded-vowel reading as “God made them blind and deaf,” comparing it to being struck with a spear or a knee.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وعموا وصموا بالضم على تقدير عماهم الله وصمهم أي: رماهم بالعمى والصمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān prefers parsing “many of them” as a substitute for the preceding pronoun; alternatives include a subject with a plural-marker dialect or an implied subject/predicate construction, which he deems weak.
rows.anchor: وارتفاع كثير على البدل من المضمر

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads “many of them” in the accusative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة: كثيرا منهم بالنصب
